concept.name: RBAC Policy Design

relationships.description: Connects RBAC Policy Design to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) decouples permissions from individual users by grouping privileges into named roles, simplifying least-privilege governance and auditing at scale.
spark.keyTakeaway: Model roles around stable job functions—not ad-hoc org charts—enforce deny-by-default evaluation with Separation of Duties (SoD), and shift fine-grained resource-level checks to ABAC/ReBAC before RBAC explodes into thousands of bespoke roles.

concept.whyItMatters: Direct user-to-permission ACLs become unmanageable past a few dozen employees: onboarding, role changes, and offboarding turn into error-prone manual diffs that leave orphaned admin rights behind. Clean RBAC turns access reviews and SOC 2 / ISO 27001 audits into deterministic queries.
whenToUse: Enterprise SaaS, internal platforms, and infrastructure control planes (AWS IAM, Kubernetes RBAC) with clear functional personas like Viewer, Editor, BillingAdmin, and Operator.
Regulated environments requiring provable Separation of Duties (SoD)—for example, preventing the same user from both creating and approving a wire transfer.
Coarse-to-medium granularity authorization where permissions depend on *who* the principal is and *what action* they perform on a resource type.
whenNotToUse: Consumer sharing or document collaboration (e.g., Google Drive 'shared with Alice, inherited by folder')—use Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC / Zanzibar).
Dynamic contextual rules like 'allow access only from corporate VPN between 09:00-17:00 for resources tagged EU-West'—layer ABAC (e.g., OPA/Cedar) alongside RBAC.
Micro-permissions tied to individual row IDs across millions of records, which causes catastrophic role explosion if modeled as roles.
keyPoints: NIST RBAC defines four tiers: Core (User-Role-Permission), Hierarchical (role inheritance), Static SoD (mutually exclusive role assignment), and Dynamic SoD (mutually exclusive active session roles).
Deny-by-default evaluation: a request is rejected unless an explicit allow matches `(subject_roles, action, resource_scope)` and no explicit deny overrides it.
Keep roles scoped to tenants/namespaces (e.g., Kubernetes `Role` + `RoleBinding` per namespace rather than `ClusterRoleBinding`) to contain blast radius.
Avoid stuffing hundreds of fine-grained permissions into JWTs; tokens hit 4-8 KB HTTP header limits and cannot be revoked immediately on role downgrade.
Decouple policy decisions from application code using a Policy Decision Point (PDP) like Open Policy Agent (OPA) or AWS Cedar.

examples.title: Kubernetes Namespace Isolation with RBAC
examples.scenario: A 40-team platform runs shared EKS clusters. Initially, developers were granted `cluster-admin` to debug pods, leading to accidental cross-team secret reads.
examples.outcome: Migrating to namespace-scoped `Role` definitions (`pods/log`, `deployments` read/write) bound via OIDC group `RoleBinding`s eliminated cross-namespace lateral movement and passed SOC 2 audit.

examples.title: OPA + Rego for Multi-Tenant SaaS Authorization
examples.scenario: A B2B SaaS app hardcoded `if (user.role === 'ADMIN')` checks across 120 microservices, causing inconsistent enforcement and slow compliance updates.
examples.outcome: Centralizing RBAC role-to-permission mappings in OPA sidecars (`< 1 ms` local Rego evaluation, bundles synced every 30s) unified audit logging and cut policy rollout time from 2 weeks to 5 minutes.

tradeOffs.pro: Coarse roles (4-8 per product) are easy to understand, assign, and audit.
tradeOffs.con: Can over-grant privileges when a user only needs one specific action; splitting into micro-roles causes role explosion.

tradeOffs.factor: Stateless JWT Claims vs. Stateful PDP Lookup
tradeOffs.pro: Embedding roles in JWTs avoids a network call on every API request.
tradeOffs.con: Role revocations lag until token expiry (often 15-60 min) and large role lists bloat HTTP headers past 8 KB.

tradeOffs.pro: Hierarchical inheritance (`Admin > Editor > Viewer`) eliminates duplicate permission lists.
tradeOffs.con: Deep inheritance chains obscure effective permissions and can accidentally grant sensitive actions (e.g., `billing:delete`) via inheritance.

failureModes.name: Role Explosion
failureModes.description: Teams create bespoke roles for every edge-case combination (`ProjectA_ReadOnly_NoExport_EU`), ballooning to thousands of un-auditable roles.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap base roles to core job functions and express resource/environment filters via ABAC attributes or scoped bindings.

failureModes.name: Privilege Creep & Stale Bindings
failureModes.description: Employees transfer teams and accumulate new roles without losing old ones, leaving long-tenured accounts with near-admin access.
failureModes.mitigation: Automate role lifecycle via SCIM/IdP group sync and enforce quarterly access recertification with auto-expiry.

failureModes.name: Confused Deputy / Cross-Tenant IDOR
failureModes.description: A service checks that `user` has role `Editor`, but forgets to verify that `resource.tenant_id == user.tenant_id`, allowing cross-tenant tampering.
failureModes.mitigation: Require tenant/resource scope as a mandatory parameter in every PDP authorization query (`allow(subject, action, tenant_id, resource)`).

failureModes.name: Stale Permission Cache After Revocation
failureModes.description: An offboarded or demoted user retains access for hours because role memberships are cached in long-lived JWTs or local memory.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep access token TTLs short (5-15 min), store only `user_id`/`session_id` in JWTs, and push revocation events to PDP caches.

commonMistakes: Mixing authentication (who you are) with authorization (what you can do) by trusting client-supplied role headers.
Using `ClusterRole` or wildcard `*:*` permissions in production workloads because scoped rules felt tedious during prototyping.
Implementing `allow`-only logic without an explicit `deny` precedence rule for emergency lockouts or SoD constraints.
Failing to log both `ALLOW` and `DENY` decisions with `subject`, `role`, `action`, `resource`, and `policy_version` for forensic audits.
Checking RBAC only at the API gateway while leaving internal gRPC/GraphQL endpoints unguarded against lateral calls.

sections.content:
## The idea

RBAC introduces an indirection layer—the **Role**—between **Principals** (users, service accounts) and **Permissions** (`action` + `resource_type`). Instead of maintaining $U \times P$ direct edges, administrators maintain $U \to R$ assignments and $R \to P$ definitions, reducing management complexity from $O(U \cdot P)$ to $O(U + P)$ when roles represent stable organizational functions.

A production RBAC engine enforces three invariants: **deny-by-default** (no matching allow means reject), **explicit deny wins** (an explicit deny or Separation-of-Duties rule overrides any allow), and **scoped bindings** (a role grants power only within a bounded tenant, project, or namespace).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a multi-tenant CI/CD platform evaluating `POST /tenants/acme/pipelines/deploy` from user `alice`:

1. **Authentication (PEP)**: The API gateway validates Alice's OIDC JWT, extracting `sub = user:alice` and `tenant = acme` (no raw permissions are trusted from the client).
2. **Authorization query**: The service's Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) sends `{subject: "user:alice", action: "pipeline:deploy", resource: {type: "pipeline", tenant: "acme", env: "prod"}}` to a co-located OPA sidecar (PDP).
3. **Role resolution**: OPA looks up Alice's scoped bindings in `acme`: `[role:deployer, role:viewer]`.
4. **Constraint & SoD check**: OPA verifies `role:deployer` includes `pipeline:deploy`, confirms no explicit `deny` applies, and checks the Dynamic SoD rule (`alice` is not the `pr_author` on this commit).
5. **Decision & audit**: OPA returns `{allow: true, matched_role: "deployer", policy_rev: "v42"}` in `< 0.5 ms` and ships an immutable decision log to SIEM.

sections.content:
## Evolving beyond pure RBAC (ABAC & ReBAC)

Pure RBAC struggles when authorization depends on **resource attributes** (`env == prod`, `classification == pii`) or **object-graph relationships** (`document -> parent_folder -> team`).

- **RBAC + ABAC hybrid**: Keep 5-10 clean functional roles (`Viewer`, `Operator`, `Admin`), and attach attribute conditions to the binding or policy (e.g., `role == Operator && resource.region == user.region`). AWS IAM and Cedar excel at this.
- **RBAC + ReBAC**: When permissions cascade through hierarchies (orgs, folders, shared links), pair top-level RBAC roles with a Zanzibar-style relationship graph (e.g., SpiceDB / OpenFGA) rather than minting per-folder roles.

## Authorization models compared

| Model | Core Primitive | Granularity | Strengths | Main Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ACL | `(User, Perm)` per object | Per-resource | Simple for tiny systems | Un-auditable at scale; hard to offboard |
| Pure RBAC | `User -> Role -> Perm` | Role / Namespace | Clean audits, SoD support, low cognitive load | Role explosion on fine-grained or contextual rules |
| ABAC (OPA / Cedar) | Attributes of subject, resource, env | Attribute-level | Expressive contextual rules without new roles | Harder to answer 'who has access to X?' upfront |
| ReBAC (Zanzibar) | Graph tuples `(obj, rel, user)` | Per-object & inherited | Models folders, teams, and sharing naturally | Requires graph store and consistency tokens (Zookies) |

## Failure modes

- **Role explosion**: Encoding tenant IDs, regions, or single-feature toggles as distinct roles creates thousands of roles that nobody understands.
- **Missing tenant-scope binding**: Checking `hasRole('Admin')` globally without binding the role to `tenant_id` enables trivial cross-tenant privilege escalation.
- **Privilege creep**: Users accumulate roles across internal transfers; without automated SCIM deprovisioning, dormant admin rights persist.
- **JWT permission bloat**: Packing all permissions into access tokens breaks 8 KB HTTP header limits and delays revocation until token expiry.

## Production patterns & governance

- **Policy-as-Code with CI tests**: Store role definitions and Rego/Cedar policies in Git; block merges unless negative tests (`deny` cases, SoD violations, cross-tenant isolation) pass.
- **Break-glass emergency roles**: Provision time-bound (e.g., 1-hour TTL) elevated roles that require ticket justification and page security on activation.
- **Shadow policy rollout**: Run new policies in `audit` mode alongside active rules to verify zero unintended `DENY` spikes on production traffic before flipping to `enforce`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enforce `deny-by-default` and `explicit-deny-overrides-allow` across all external and internal endpoints.
- [ ] Bind every role assignment to an explicit scope (`tenant_id`, `namespace`, or `project_id`).
- [ ] Keep JWTs thin (identity + session); resolve fine-grained roles via a local PDP sidecar or short-TTL cache.
- [ ] Encode Static and Dynamic Separation of Duties (SoD) for high-risk actions (deploy, billing, key rotation).
- [ ] Integrate SCIM/IdP lifecycle sync and log every allow/deny decision with `policy_version`.

interviewProblems.title: RBAC Policy Design
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on RBAC Policy Design. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) decouples permissions from individual users by grouping privileges into named roles, simplifying least-privilege governance and auditing at scale.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: OPA Sidecar (PDP) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Policy Bundle & Audit.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Policy Bundle & Audit experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Cap base roles to core job functions and express resource/environment filters via ABAC attributes or scoped bindings.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Model roles around stable job functions—not ad-hoc org charts—enforce deny-by-default evaluation with Separation of Duties (SoD), and shift fine-grained resource-level checks to ABAC/ReBAC before RBAC explodes into thousands of bespoke roles.
Avoid trap: Mixing authentication (who you are) with authorization (what you can do) by trusting client-supplied role headers.
Avoid trap: Using `ClusterRole` or wildcard `*:*` permissions in production workloads because scoped rules felt tedious during prototyping.
When to reach for it: Enterprise SaaS, internal platforms, and infrastructure control planes (AWS IAM, Kubernetes RBAC) with clear functional personas like Viewer, Editor, BillingAdmin, and Operator.
When to reach for it: Regulated environments requiring provable Separation of Duties (SoD)—for example, preventing the same user from both creating and approving a wire transfer.

putItTogether.title: Putting Rbac Policy Design Together
putItTogether.summary: Model roles around stable job functions—not ad-hoc org charts—enforce deny-by-default evaluation with Separation of Duties (SoD), and shift fine-grained resource-level checks to ABAC/ReBAC before RBAC explodes into thousands of bespoke roles.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Rbac Policy Design before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Migrating to namespace-scoped `Role` definitions (`pods/log`, `deployments` read/write) bound via OIDC group `RoleBinding`s eliminated cross-namespace lateral movement and passed SOC 2 audit.
